ui.farDiagram: Lagrange points and missions beyond Earth
ui.title: Earth-protecting satellites
ui.lead: Each icon sits on the kind of orbit its mission uses. Low Earth orbit is the inner ring, then medium, geostationary, and a long ellipse for highly elliptical orbits. Distances are not to scale, so every ring stays visible. Nothing here is a live position.
ui.scale: The ring order follows NASA Earth Observatory’s Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits and the Earth-centered style of NASA Eyes on the Earth. Imagery: NASA Visible Earth / Blue Marble Next Generation. Created by the Founder and SI.
ui.helpsPage: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.
ui.explain1: A Lagrange point is a place where the gravity of the Sun and the Earth lines up with the motion of an orbit, so a spacecraft can keep pace with Earth. NASA says the pull of the two large masses equals the centripetal force a small object needs to move with them. There are five. L1, L2, and L3 sit on the Sun–Earth line and are unstable. L4 leads Earth and L5 follows, at the tips of equilateral triangles, and those two are stable.
ui.explain2: L1 and L2 are each about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth. NASA’s Webb orbit page rounds that to 1 million miles, which is about 930,000 miles if you convert 1.5 million kilometers directly. L1 faces the Sun, so SOHO and DSCOVR get a steady view of it. L2 is on the night side, a cold and steady spot for telescopes such as Webb, Euclid, and Roman. A spacecraft does not sit on the point. It loops around the point in a halo or Lissajous orbit.
ui.explain3: Webb’s trip started with launch on an Ariane 5 on 25 December 2021. NASA says that launch put Webb on a transfer path of about 30 days. Three mid-course correction burns refined the path, and the last one, on 24 January 2022, pointed Webb into its halo orbit. Because L1, L2, and L3 are unstable, Webb fires small station-keeping burns, on average about every 42 days, or it would drift away. L4 and L5 do not need that kind of care. L3 stays hidden behind the Sun, about 1 AU from the Sun and about 2 AU from Earth. L4 and L5 are about 1 AU from Earth, 60 degrees ahead and behind. This drawing is not to scale. NASA’s Moon fact sheet lists a mean distance of 384,400 km (238,855 miles).
ui.dL12: about 1.5 million km · about 1 million miles
ui.dL3: about 2 AU from Earth · far side of the Sun

sats.name: Landsat 9 (NASA / USGS)
sats.does: Landsat 9 continues a 50-year record of Earth’s land, collecting 740 scenes a day and, with Landsat 8, seeing each place every 8 days.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Copernicus Sentinel-2C (ESA)
sats.does: Sentinel-2C joined the Copernicus fleet in September 2024, imaging land and coasts in 13 bands so forests and crops are checked every five days.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: NISAR (NASA–ISRO)
sats.does: NISAR, a NASA and ISRO radar satellite launched from India on July 30, 2025, scans nearly all of Earth's land and ice twice every 12 days, even through clouds.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Biomass (ESA)
sats.does: ESA's Biomass satellite, launched April 29, 2025, carries the first P-band radar in space, seeing through forest canopies to measure the carbon stored in trees.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: ALOS-4 "DAICHI-4" (JAXA)
sats.does: JAXA's DAICHI-4 radar sees through clouds over a 200 km swath, continuing the radar record used for deforestation alerts.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: SMAP Soil Moisture Active Passive (NASA)
sats.does: SMAP maps the water in Earth's soil from space, helping improve predictions of weather, floods and droughts (NASA).
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: PACE (NASA)
sats.does: NASA's PACE reads the color of the ocean to track phytoplankton, the base of the marine food web, plus aerosols and clouds.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: SWOT (NASA–CNES)
sats.does: SWOT measures more than 95% of Earth's lakes larger than 15 acres and rivers wider than 330 feet, the first global survey of fresh water.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Copernicus Sentinel-6B (ESA / NASA)
sats.does: Sentinel-6B, launched November 17, 2025, continues the precise record of global sea level that began in the early 1990s.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: EOS-06 / Oceansat-3 (ISRO)
sats.does: India's EOS-06, the third Oceansat, tracks ocean color, sea-surface temperature and winds; it imaged Cyclone Mandous and an algal bloom on day one.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Copernicus Sentinel-3 (ESA / EUMETSAT)
sats.does: The Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellites measure Earth's oceans, land, ice and atmosphere, and a third satellite, Sentinel-3C, launched on September 15, 2026.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: ICESat-2 (NASA)
sats.does: NASA's ICESat-2 laser fires 10,000 pulses a second to measure ice sheets, sea ice, forests and coastal seafloor in 3D. Active.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: CryoSat Ice Mission (ESA)
sats.does: CryoSat measures polar sea ice and the great ice sheets from space, and its data revealed 85 hidden lakes under Antarctica (ESA).
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Arctic Weather Satellite and EPS-Sterna (ESA/EUMETSAT)
sats.does: ESA's small Arctic Weather Satellite, launched in August 2024, paved the way for EPS-Sterna, a fleet of 20 satellites from 2029 (ESA, EUMETSAT).
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: PREFIRE Polar CubeSats (NASA)
sats.does: Two shoebox-size NASA satellites measure the far-infrared heat that Earth's poles send into space (NASA JPL). Last reviewed: October 2026 · 4 sources cited
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: GOES-19 and CCOR-1 (NOAA)
sats.does: NOAA's GOES-19 carries CCOR-1, the world's first operational space-based coronagraph, imaging the Sun's corona every 15 minutes.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: INSAT-3DS Weather Satellite (ISRO)
sats.does: India's INSAT-3DS watches weather, land and oceans from geostationary orbit and carries a search-and-rescue transponder (ISRO).
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Meteosat Third Generation (ESA / EUMETSAT)
sats.does: Three weather satellites now watch Europe and Africa from 36,000 km up, with new images every 2.5 minutes and a camera that catches lightning day and…
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: TEMPO Air Quality Mission (NASA)
sats.does: From geostationary orbit, NASA's TEMPO measures air pollution over North America every daylight hour, a first from space (NASA).
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: OCO-2 Orbiting Carbon Observatory (NASA)
sats.does: NASA's OCO-2 satellite has measured carbon dioxide around the planet since 2014, showing where carbon is released and where forests and oceans absorb it.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: FireSat (Earth Fire Alliance)
sats.does: Earth Fire Alliance's FireSat satellites are built to spot wildfires as small as 5 by 5 meters from space and get the data to firefighters fast.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: NEOSSat Asteroid and Debris Telescope (Canada)
sats.does: Canada's NEOSSat circles Earth every 100 minutes, scanning near the Sun for asteroids and comets and tracking satellites and debris (CSA).
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Galileo Satellite Navigation (EU / ESA)
sats.does: Europe's Galileo is the world's most precise satellite navigation system, serving over five billion smartphone users and helping rescues (ESA).
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Hubble Space Telescope
sats.does: NASA lists Hubble as an extended mission in low Earth orbit. A January 2026 Space Telescope Science Institute status said it was operating in reduced-gyro mode.
sats.helps: Hubble has measured what some atmospheres of planets around other stars are made of (NASA). That is a comparison, not a watch on Earth.

sats.name: Chandra X-ray Observatory
sats.does: NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, run day to day by the Smithsonian, flies a highly elliptical Earth orbit out to about 139,000 km. A Chandra status report on 2 October 2026 said it had completed that week’s observing schedule.
sats.helps: Chandra shows exploding stars and hot gas, the violent settings in which planetary systems form. It does not watch Earth’s weather.

sats.name: TESS
sats.does: NASA’s TESS surveys the sky for planets that pass in front of nearby stars. It flies a high Earth orbit.
sats.helps: Finding those planets is the first step before anyone can ask whether they keep an atmosphere. TESS does not monitor Earth.

sats.name: James Webb Space Telescope
sats.does: How the James Webb Space Telescope tracked asteroid 2024 YR4 in February 2026 and ruled out a 2032 Moon impact, two years before ground telescopes could.
sats.helps: That page says Webb ruled out a 2032 impact on the Moon. NASA also uses Webb to study atmospheres of planets around other stars. It is not an Earth-monitoring satellite.
sats.credit: Photo: NASA. James Webb Space Telescope primary mirror fully assembled.

sats.name: Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope
sats.does: NASA's Roman telescope launched Aug 30, 2026 to L2: Hubble-sharp images 100x wider, a census of planetary systems, first images by early 2027.
sats.helps: Roman is built for a wide census of planetary systems and a coronagraph that practices photographing planets around other stars. It is not yet in routine science operations.
sats.credit: Photo: NASA. Roman lifts off, 30 August 2026.

sats.name: Euclid
sats.does: ESA’s Euclid, with NASA contributions, launched on 1 July 2023 to Sun–Earth L2 and is in operation (CNES mission sheet).
sats.helps: Euclid maps dark matter and dark energy. It does not study Earth’s air or oceans. It describes the universe planets sit in.
sats.credit: Photo: NASA/JPL-Caltech (PIA25783). Euclid spacecraft in a clean room.

sats.name: SOHO Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (ESA / NASA)
sats.does: Watching the Sun nonstop since 1995, SOHO helps experts predict solar storms and has found more than 5,000 comets (NASA).
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: Aditya-L1 (ISRO)
sats.does: Aditya-L1 is ISRO's first space-based solar observatory, studying the Sun from a halo orbit around L1, about 1.5 million km from Earth.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.

sats.name: DSCOVR / EPIC (NASA–NOAA)
sats.does: NASA's EPIC camera rides on NOAA's DSCOVR spacecraft at the L1 point, photographing the entire sunlit face of Earth several times a day, with an archive...
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.
sats.credit: Photo: NASA. DSCOVR spacecraft at Kennedy Space Center.

sats.name: IMAP (NASA)
sats.does: NASA's IMAP watches the Sun from about a million miles sunward and can give about a half hour's warning of incoming radiation.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.
sats.credit: Photo: NASA. IMAP spacecraft at Kennedy Space Center.

sats.name: NEO Surveyor
sats.does: NASA NEO Surveyor is the first space telescope built to find hazardous asteroids, including dark ones hidden in the Sun's glare. Launch NET September 2027.
sats.helps: The sentence above is the mission page on this site. We do not add a broader claim than that page.
sats.credit: Photo: NASA (PIA26711). NEO Surveyor spacecraft bus during a test, not the finished observatory.

sats.name: Europa Clipper
sats.does: NASA's Europa Clipper is on its way to Jupiter's ocean moon, with an Earth gravity assist on December 3, 2026 and 49 close Europa flybys from 2030.
sats.helps: The mission page says it is on the way to Jupiter’s ocean moon, with an Earth gravity assist on 3 December 2026 and close Europa flybys from 2030. It studies another ocean world, not Earth’s oceans.
sats.credit: Photo: NASA (PIA25125). Europa Clipper during assembly.

sats.name: Juice
sats.does: ESA's Juice will study Ganymede, Callisto and Europa, with 35 moon flybys after it reaches Jupiter in July 2031. Cruising.
sats.helps: The mission page says Juice is cruising and will study Ganymede, Callisto and Europa after reaching Jupiter in July 2031. That is comparative planetology, not an Earth forecast.

sats.name: Psyche
sats.does: NASA's Psyche used a Mars flyby on 15 May 2026 to head for a metal-rich asteroid it will orbit from August 2029, to learn what a planet's core is like.
sats.helps: The mission page says a Mars flyby on 15 May 2026 sent Psyche toward a metal-rich asteroid it will orbit from August 2029, to learn what a planet’s core can be like.
sats.credit: Photo: NASA. Psyche spacecraft at Astrotech.

sats.name: Hera
sats.does: ESA's Hera arrives at the asteroid Dimorphos in November 2026 to measure what NASA's DART impact did, turning deflection into a repeatable defense.
sats.helps: The mission page says Hera arrives at Dimorphos in November 2026 to measure what NASA’s DART impact did. That is a planetary-defense measurement, and the arrival date is the one the page states.
sats.credit: Artist's concept (ESA – Science Office, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO).
